title: The Power of Nearing the Finish Line
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Using the image of marathoners who speed up in the final mile, this article explains the psychological phenomenon of goal proximity: people push harder as a finish line comes into view, even when logic suggests fatigue should slow them down. The author gives everyday leadership examples -- salespeople chasing quotas, employees eyeing a promotion -- to show the effect at work across contexts. A practical threshold is offered: once a project crosses roughly 80 percent completion, naming that proximity aloud can galvanize a team's final push. The piece closes by noting the effect holds even when people are aware it's happening, making it a reliable lever for leaders.
points: The 'goal proximity effect' explains why effort and focus intensify as a deadline or finish line nears.
Leaders can trigger this effect deliberately by explicitly pointing out when a project is close to completion.
A rough rule of thumb: start naming the approaching finish line once a project passes about 80 percent done.
The effect applies to personal goals too, from diet and exercise routines to finishing a book or a course.
Awareness of the effect doesn't cancel it out -- people still push harder even when they know why.
quotes: Marathon runners normally run the 26th mile faster than most of the miles preceding it.
The closer we get to a goal, the more effort we make to realize our success.
Academics call this effect goal proximity, and it exerts a powerful influence on how we conclude a project, initiative or design.
A good rule of thumb is to begin speaking about the finish line when the percentage of work completed passes 80 percent.
The goal proximity effect exists even when we know of its influence.
